title: SWIFT: Self-guided Weak-to-strong dIFfusion models via Target extrapolation

paper.abstract: Abstract Training high-quality diffusion models is computationally expensive, and inference-time guidance often adds further sampling cost. In this work, we introduce Swift , a simple yet effective self-guided training method that uses a frozen weak denoiser to improve a stronger model without adding inference overhead. For each noisy input, Swift extrapolates the clean regression target away from the weak denoiser’s prediction, amplifying components that remain underfit. The weak guide can be an early training checkpoint, requires no backpropagation during main-model training, and is discarded afterward. The resulting model retains the original sampler and supports both conditional and unconditional generation without label dropout or an unconditional branch. We explain this mechanism through a spectral analysis of finite-time population gradient flow in an RKHS. With an early-stopped weak guide, we prove that a nonempty range of extrapolation strengths yields strictly lower posterior-mean error than matched standard training, despite shifting the regression target away from the posterior mean. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-256 demonstrate improvements across model scales and representations. In one ImageNet-256 configuration, Swift surpasses the baseline’s best FID using roughly half the total training compute, including guide preparation and training overhead. On RAEv2, it achieves FID 1.15 1.15 without inference-time guidance and 0.99 with guidance. These results establish target extrapolation as an effective approach to weak-to-strong diffusion training with efficient single-model inference.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models have achieved strong generative performance across images, video, and audio [ 8 , 9 , 12 ] . They are typically trained with a simple denoising regression objective, yet many of the strongest generation results rely on guidance applied only at inference [ 7 , 11 ] . In particular, autoguidance [ 11 ] shows that a deliberately weaker denoiser can improve a stronger one by defining an extrapolation direction during sampling. This suggests a broader role for weak models: rather than serving as teachers to imitate, they can provide directions along which a stronger predictor should move. Autoguidance realizes this idea by extrapolating the strong model’s prediction away from that of a smaller or less-trained counterpart [ 11 ] . Related training-time approaches instead use evolving model predictions, intermediate supervision, or guidance-conditioned objectives [ 28 , 39 , 2 , 36 ] ( Section 8 ). These developments motivate a simple question: Can weak-to-strong extrapolation be moved from inference into training, so that the final denoiser itself benefits from the correction and the weak model can be discarded afterward? We introduce Swift , a self-guided training method that uses a frozen weak denoiser to construct extrapolated regression targets. For each noisy input, instead of regressing directly toward the clean sample, Swift moves the target farther in the direction from the weak prediction toward and beyond the clean sample. The weak denoiser therefore acts as a directional reference , rather than a teacher whose output should be imitated. It can be obtained from an early checkpoint of ordinary denoising training, remains fixed during the main training run, and requires no backpropagation. After training, the guide is discarded, leaving a single denoiser and the original sampling procedure. The same construction applies to both conditional and unconditional generation. Our motivation is finite-time underfitting: because a weak denoiser has learned less of the target function, extrapolating away from its prediction can amplify directions that remain underfit. Our RAEv2/DINOv3-L model reaches 1.15 1.15 gFID without inference-time guidance and 0.99 0.99 with retuned internal guidance ( Section 11.3 ). Right: on the matched RAE/DINOv2-B configuration [ 30 , 38 , 22 ] , the advantage of Swift persists throughout extended training ( Section 11.4 ). Dots denote raw evaluations and lines show five-point moving averages. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-256 show that the effect is not tied to a particular representation or model family. On ImageNet-256, Swift improves diffusion models built on conventional VAE latents, representation-autoencoder latents [ 38 , 26 ] , end-to-end learned latent representations, and direct pixel-space generation. Across the evaluated DiffusionBench configurations [ 16 ] , the same fixed Swift recipe lowers unguided FID in every configuration, and the improvement persists under longer training. The complete ImageNet comparisons and training trajectories are in Sections 11.1 and 11.4 , and the additional CIFAR-10 experiments are in Section 12 . Swift also remains complementary to inference-time guidance. When guidance is independently retuned for the baseline and Swift , the Swift model achieves lower FID in every tested configuration ( Tables 7 and 10.2 ). Moreover, on RAEv2 the preferred internal-guidance scale decreases from 1.78 1.78 for the baseline to 1.20 1.20 after Swift training, while the best guided gFID improves from 1.04 1.04 to 0.99 0.99 ( Figure 4 (b) ; Section 11.3 ). This is consistent with Swift internalizing part of the weak-to-strong correction during training while leaving additional room for inference-time guidance. Our contributions are: • Weak-to-strong learning through target extrapolation. We introduce Swift , which uses a frozen weak denoiser as a directional reference to extrapolate clean-sample regression targets. The guide is fixed during main-model training and discarded at inference ( Section 2.2 ). • Broad improvements across diffusion representations. We demonstrate consistent gains across CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-256, spanning VAE, RAE, end-to-end latent, and pixel-space diffusion models. The gains persist under longer training and remain after inference-time guidance is independently retuned ( Sections 5.1 and 5.2 ). • A finite-training explanation. We show theoretically that target extrapolation can strictly reduce posterior-mean error relative to matched standard training over a nonempty range of positive extrapolation strengths ( Section 4 ).

sections.heading: Constructing the frozen weak denoiser.
sections.text: We train 𝒟 weak \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{weak}} in the ordinary way with Eq. 1 and freeze it before the main run. The default guide uses a smaller architecture; capacity and training-stage variants are studied separately. The default DiffusionBench guide has approximately one quarter as many parameters as the main denoiser and is trained for half the main model’s standard training duration; the CIFAR-10 and RAEv2 guide checkpoints are specified in Section 10.1 . The method is self-guided because the correction comes from a weaker denoiser trained on the same task, without an external teacher, a separate guidance objective, or an auxiliary prediction head. The intuition is to compensate for what ordinary training has not learned within a finite training budget. Extrapolating the clean target away from 𝒟 weak \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{weak}} emphasizes directions in which the weak denoiser’s prediction remains inaccurate. Whether this improves the main denoiser’s approximation to the posterior mean depends on how those directions relate to its own finite-training error. For a frozen weak denoiser obtained by early stopping ordinary training, Sections 4 and 4.1 establish conditions under which Swift achieves strictly lower posterior-mean error than baseline training (proofs in Section 7 ; a Gaussian-mixture illustration is in Section 9 ).

sections.heading: Training and inference.
sections.text: During training, only the main denoiser 𝒟 𝜽 \mathcal{D}_{\bm{\theta}} is optimized with Eq. 4 . The weak denoiser 𝒟 weak \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{weak}} is evaluated without gradients and remains fixed. Thus, for a fixed clean sample, noise realization, and noise level, the regression target does not change as the main denoiser is updated. Beyond preparing the weak denoiser, each training step requires one additional weak-denoiser forward pass (about 9 % 9\% more FLOPs on DiffusionBench; Section 10.3 ). After training, it is discarded; sampling uses the trained denoiser and the original sampler, with no additional inference-time model evaluation ( Section 10.2 ).

sections.heading: 3.2 Comparison with Training-Based Guidance
sections.text: MG constructs a training correction using conditional and unconditional model predictions [ 28 ] . SGG studies incorporating guidance into training using an updated weak network or an intermediate prediction branch in its training-time variants [ 36 ] . GFT trains across guidance strengths using an unconditional prediction [ 2 ] . In these constructions, the auxiliary predictions can change as their models are trained. IG jointly supervises intermediate and final outputs for sampling-time guidance; it also studies training with a detached final-minus-intermediate EMA correction [ 39 , Sec. 6] . These designs use a changing prediction in the training correction or supervise an additional output. Swift obtains 𝒟 weak \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{weak}} by ordinary denoising training and freezes it before training the main denoiser. For a fixed training example and noise realization, its extrapolated target does not change as the main model is updated. This avoids joint optimization of the weak and main denoisers, which provided no clear additional endpoint benefit in our CIFAR-10 comparisons ( Section 12 ), and leaves a single denoiser at inference. Preparing and evaluating the weak denoiser still incur training compute, which our compute comparisons account for ( Section 10.3 ). Further methodological details appear in Sections 8 , B.2 and B.3 .

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate Swift on ImageNet-256 [ 3 ] and CIFAR-10 [ 13 ] . In every experiment Swift changes only the regression target; architectures, training schedules, samplers, and evaluation pipelines are kept the same as the baseline. sections.heading: Choosing α \alpha .
sections.text: Performance is broadly U-shaped in α \alpha ( Figure 6 (a) ). On CIFAR-10, moderate positive values form a broad favorable region around α = 0.7 \alpha=0.7 – 0.9 0.9 , where differences are comparable to replicate noise. ImageNet shows the same qualitative behavior: on DINOv2-B, α ∈ [ 0.5 , 1.0 ] \alpha\in[0.5,1.0] substantially improves over the baseline. The precise optimum depends on the model, however, so our breadth experiments use the fixed default α = 0.4 \alpha=0.4 without tuning; in practice, a small sweep over moderate positive values is sufficient. Negative α \alpha can accelerate the initial decrease in FID, but the tested negative warm starts provide no consistent final-quality advantage ( Section 12 ).

sections.heading: Choosing the weak guide.
sections.text: The guide should be weaker than the student, but still competent. At α = 0.8 \alpha=0.8 on CIFAR-10, reducing the channel base from the student’s 128 to 64 improves FID from 2.58 2.58 to 1.60 1.60 , while substantially smaller guides degrade rapidly ( Figure 6 (b) ). The half-width guide is also the best width across the tested α \alpha values on CIFAR-10 and consistently outperforms wider alternatives on ImageNet. Guide training length shows a similar pattern: once the guide crosses a competence threshold, performance is relatively insensitive over a broad range ( Figure 6 (c) ). On ImageNet, freezing the guide earlier can even help, with an earlier guide outperforming the default guide in our 50k re-evaluation; the corresponding training trajectories are discussed in Section 11.4 .

sections.heading: A simple fixed recipe gives substantial gains.
sections.text: The full CIFAR-10 campaign also tests jointly trained guides, capacity switches, and coefficients that change with training time or noise level ( Sections 12 and 10 ). Co-training provides no clear additional endpoint benefit in the tested comparisons. Some early capacity switches and late coefficient profiles give useful CIFAR-10 refinements, whereas other schedules lose the gain; their effects depend on the guide and coefficient, and many small differences remain unresolved by repetitions. We therefore retain a frozen half-width guide and a fixed, moderate positive α \alpha as the simple default for the broader experiments.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: The regression target has received comparatively little attention as a design choice in diffusion training, yet it turns out to be a simple and effective place to intervene. By carrying the clean target past itself and away from a frozen weak model, Swift moves a weak-to-strong correction from inference into training, leaving a single denoiser and the original sampler at deployment with only about 9 % 9\% additional main-training FLOPs. Crucially, the modified target is not itself a better estimator of the posterior mean: it is deliberately biased, yet finite training on it can produce a better final predictor and better samples. This suggests a broader view of the regression target as a design interface rather than a fixed quantity—and raises the question of what other useful corrections can be written into it.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: Swift changes only the regression target: the objective is Eqs. 4 and 5 , the frozen weak denoiser is constructed as described in Section 2.2 , and everything else is the training loop of the respective framework. Section 10.1 specifies guide architectures, freezing points, coefficients, training budgets, and hardware for the EDM, DiffusionBench, and RAEv2 models, and explains the velocity-target implementation. Section 10.2 specifies samplers, guidance and checkpoint selection, and evaluation metrics, distinguishing re-evaluated pairs from published baselines; Section 10.3 reports the GPU hours and the FLOPs accounting behind Figures 1 and 5 . sections.heading: 7.9 Scope of the analysis
sections.text: The population improvement argument requires square-integrable targets, not Gaussianity. It compares fixed-noise denoising MSE at equal main-model optimization time; guide preparation and forward passes add compute. The finite-step result assumes fixed features, and the finite-sample result additionally requires conditional centering and integrability. Neural feature learning need not satisfy these conditions, and denoising MSE alone does not guarantee improved FID or iterative sampling.

sections.heading: Common notation.
sections.text: We write the diffusion objectives in one regression parameterization, suppressing inputs, expectations, and noise-dependent loss weights. Let 𝒒 \bm{q} be the sample-wise label (clean sample, noise, or velocity), 𝒇 \bm{f} the final conditional prediction, 𝒖 \bm{u} the unconditional prediction, and 𝒉 \bm{h} a supervised intermediate prediction. Bars denote EMA predictions and sg \operatorname{sg} stops gradients. All outputs and labels in each expression use the same parameterization.

sections.heading: CFG and AG: extrapolation at sampling.
sections.text: CFG retains the ordinary denoising target and trains conditional and unconditional outputs through label dropout; sampling uses 𝒇 + w ⁡ ( 𝒇 − 𝒖 ) \bm{f}+w(\bm{f}-\bm{u}) [ 7 , Algorithms 1–2] . AG also retains ordinary denoising losses, but samples with 𝒇 + α ⁡ ( 𝒇 − 𝒈 ) \bm{f}+\alpha(\bm{f}-\bm{g}) , where 𝒈 \bm{g} is a separately trained, less accurate model with the same conditioning [ 11 , Sec. 4] . AG’s frozen weak model is a sampling reference, not a target in main training.

sections.heading: MG, SGG, and IG’s training variant: prediction-gap targets.
sections.text: Their final-output losses have the form ℒ Δ = ‖ 𝒇 − [ 𝒒 + λ ​ sg ⁡ ( 𝚫 ) ] ‖ 2 2 , 𝚫 MG = 𝒇 ¯ − 𝒖 ¯ , 𝚫 SGG = { 𝒇 − 𝒖 , high noise , 𝒇 − 𝒉 , low noise , 𝚫 IG ​ - ​ train = 𝒇 ¯ − 𝒉 ¯ . \mathcal{L}_{\Delta}=\|\bm{f}-[\bm{q}+\lambda\operatorname{sg}(\bm{\Delta})]\|_{2}^{2},\qquad\begin{array}[]{@{}l@{\;}l@{}}\bm{\Delta}_{\mathrm{MG}}&{}=\bar{\bm{f}}-\bar{\bm{u}},\\ \bm{\Delta}_{\mathrm{SGG}}&{}=\begin{cases}\bm{f}-\bm{u},&\text{high noise},\\ \bm{f}-\bm{h},&\text{low noise},\end{cases}\\ \bm{\Delta}_{\mathrm{IG\text{-}train}}&{}=\bar{\bm{f}}-\bar{\bm{h}}.\end{array} (B.1) MG uses conditional/unconditional EMA predictions [ 28 , Eqs. 17–18] . SGG applies its correction within a chosen time interval, switches the weak source across noise levels, and supervises its intermediate branch against 𝒒 \bm{q} [ 36 , Sec. 4.3 and App. D.1] . The same paper’s training-time AG variant instead uses a separate small model, updated once per four main-model updates. Its strong-minus-weak correction therefore evolves during training. IG’s training variant also supervises the intermediate output and uses the EMA gap in Eq. B.1 [ 39 , Sec. 6, Eq. 7] . The entire gap, including its strong prediction, is detached in these target corrections.

sections.heading: IG’s main method: auxiliary supervision and shared-pass sampling.
sections.text: The main IG objective is ‖ 𝒇 − 𝒒 ‖ 2 2 + γ ​ ‖ 𝒉 − 𝒒 ‖ 2 2 \|\bm{f}-\bm{q}\|_{2}^{2}+\gamma\|\bm{h}-\bm{q}\|_{2}^{2} . Both losses update the shared backbone, but the final label remains 𝒒 \bm{q} . Sampling extrapolates the final and intermediate outputs from the same backbone pass [ 39 , Sec. 3.2, Eqs. 3–5] . Thus needing two outputs does not imply two full network passes.

sections.text: GFT samples β \beta and conditions the shared model on it; its practical loss mixes the sampling prediction 𝒇 β \bm{f}_{\beta} with a detached unconditional output evaluated at β = 1 \beta=1 [ 2 , Eq. 9 and Algorithm 1] : ‖ β ​ 𝒇 β + ( 1 − β ) ​ sg ⁡ ( 𝒖 ) − 𝒒 ‖ 2 2 = β 2 ​ ‖ 𝒇 β − [ 𝒒 + α ⁡ ( 𝒒 − sg ⁡ ( 𝒖 ) ) ] ‖ 2 2 , α = 1 − β β , 0 < β ≤ 1 . \|\beta\bm{f}_{\beta}+(1-\beta)\operatorname{sg}(\bm{u})-\bm{q}\|_{2}^{2}=\beta^{2}\|\bm{f}_{\beta}-[\bm{q}+\alpha(\bm{q}-\operatorname{sg}(\bm{u}))]\|_{2}^{2},\quad\alpha=\frac{1-\beta}{\beta},\quad 0<\beta\leq 1. For fixed data and noise, the target is independent of the main parameters. There is also an update-level overlap with prediction-gap training: if the strong prediction inside the gap is the current 𝒇 \bm{f} and the weak 𝒈 \bm{g} is fixed, then, for 0 ≤ w < 1 0\leq w<1 , ∇ θ ‖ 𝒇 − 𝒒 − w ​ sg ⁡ ( 𝒇 − 𝒈 ) ‖ 2 2 = ( 1 − w ) ​ ∇ θ ‖ 𝒇 − ( 1 + α ) ​ 𝒒 + α ​ 𝒈 ‖ 2 2 , α = w 1 − w . \nabla_{\theta}\|\bm{f}-\bm{q}-w\operatorname{sg}(\bm{f}-\bm{g})\|_{2}^{2}=(1-w)\nabla_{\theta}\|\bm{f}-(1+\alpha)\bm{q}+\alpha\bm{g}\|_{2}^{2},\qquad\alpha=\frac{w}{1-w}. sections.heading: 10 Experimental Setup
sections.text: We specify training ( Section 10.1 ), evaluation ( Section 10.2 ), and compute accounting ( Section 10.3 ). In matched comparisons, Swift changes only the training target, leaving the model’s architecture, optimizer, schedule, sampler, and evaluator fixed. In the default frozen-guide recipe, the guide receives the same noisy image (or latent), noise level, and class condition as the main denoiser. Its prediction is evaluated without gradients and used only to construct the target in Eq. 5 ; the original noise distribution, loss weighting, and optimizer update are retained. The frozen guide is not an inference-time component.

sections.heading: CIFAR-10.
sections.text: We use the EDM configuration of Karras et al. [10] : a class-conditional DDPM++ model at 32 × 32 32\times 32 resolution with EDM preconditioning and loss weighting, batch size 512, fp32 training, and a 200,000 200{,}000 -kimg horizon ( kimg = 10 3 \mathrm{kimg}=10^{3} training images). The main denoiser uses channel base 128 ( cb128 ). Guide capacity is specified by channel base ( cb16 – cb128 ), with cb64 denoting the default half-width guide. NCSN++ and ADM-style guide variants use the corresponding channel bases; their full results are reported in Section 12 . The default guide is a separately trained, class-conditional DDPM++ cb64 model frozen at 200,000 200{,}000 kimg. Unless a sweep changes it, α \alpha is a fixed scalar. The α = 0 \alpha=0 arm ( D0 ) is the ordinary-training reference at the same main-model budget and evaluation endpoint; it is not a new seed-matched baseline trained for every exploratory setting. Section 12 and the accompanying DATA/ ledger distinguish repeated runs, guide variants, and incomplete or extended runs.

sections.heading: ImageNet-256, DiffusionBench.
sections.text: Our main DiffusionBench model [ 16 ] uses a representation-autoencoder tokenizer [ 38 ] over frozen DINOv2-B features [ 22 ] and a 615M-parameter decoupled diffusion transformer [ 30 ] . The breadth study keeps the 615M-parameter training recipe while varying the tokenizer or using a pixel-space model ( Section 11.1 ). The model is trained class-conditionally with global batch size 1024 for 80 epochs, corresponding to 1251 optimizer steps per epoch, and is evaluated every five epochs. Unless stated otherwise, the 18 DiffusionBench configurations use the same Swift recipe: α = 0.4 \alpha=0.4 and a separate guide for the corresponding model, pretrained for half the main model’s standard training duration and then frozen. Each half-width guide has about 155M parameters and approximately one quarter of the main denoiser’s forward-pass FLOPs. The short-guide ablation freezes the same architecture at an earlier checkpoint. CFG is used only at sampling time and is tuned independently for the baseline and Swift . The ImageNet backends use linear flow matching, 𝒙 t = ( 1 − t ) ​ 𝒙 0 + t ​ ϵ \bm{x}_{t}=(1-t)\bm{x}_{0}+t\bm{\epsilon} and 𝒗 = ϵ − 𝒙 0 \bm{v}=\bm{\epsilon}-\bm{x}_{0} , with ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) \bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\mathbf{I}) , rather than the additive-noise parameterization of Section 2.1 . sections.heading: Guidance at sampling time.
sections.text: RAEv2’s native internal guidance obtains its weak prediction from the first 8 of the backbone’s 28 blocks ( base_model_depth=8 ), rather than from the separately pretrained Swift guide. For unguided Swift evaluation, the training guide is removed entirely. The evaluation script sets self_guide.k=0 and clears the guide list before checkpoint loading; the training guide is therefore absent from both unguided and natively guided sampling. For guided re-evaluations, CFG or internal-guidance strength is swept separately for each model; we report the best measured FID and compute other metrics on the samples from that setting. A published guided baseline is identified as such, without claiming that we retuned its scale ( Figure 7 ).

sections.heading: Checkpoint selection.
sections.text: DiffusionBench breadth results compare an 80-epoch Swift model with an 80-epoch baseline or source-reported baseline; the longer DINOv2-B pair shares an evaluation schedule. RAEv2 has a matched epoch-160 comparison, while its headline 1.15 1.15 unguided and 0.99 0.99 guided Swift values select the epoch-140 checkpoint within the 160-epoch budget ( Section 11.3 ), not a same-epoch causal comparison.

sections.heading: Metric computation.
sections.text: FID uses the training-set reference statistics of the corresponding dataset [ 6 ] . ImageNet-256 sFID, Inception Score [ 25 ] , precision, recall, FD r , and MIND use the same generated set as FID. FD r and MIND cover Inception, ConvNeXt, DINOv2, MAE, and SigLIP; Table 1 averages the five spaces. Re-evaluated pairs share metric implementations and reference features. RAEv2’s FID uses the standard ImageNet statistics; its additional representation-space comparisons use our ImageNet training-set feature bank.

sections.heading: 10.3 Compute Accounting
sections.text: We separate main-model training from the one-time guide pretraining, which can serve multiple Swift runs.

sections.heading: Wall-clock measurements.
sections.text: On 4 × 4\times B200 GPUs, 80 DiffusionBench baseline epochs take about 44 hours versus 49 hours for the Swift main run; guide pretraining takes another 12 hours once. We use FLOPs for hardware-independent comparison.

sections.heading: Per-step FLOPs.
sections.text: Analytical forward costs are 337.5 GFLOPs per sample for the main denoiser and 87.3 GFLOPs for its half-width guide, a ratio of 0.259. A baseline update uses a main-model forward pass and a backward pass estimated at twice that cost. Swift adds one frozen-guide forward pass without guide backpropagation. This raises main-training FLOPs by about 9 % 9\% per update. A PyTorch FLOP counter agrees with the full-update estimate to within 0.5 % 0.5\% .

sections.heading: Guide preparation.
sections.text: For the same number of samples per epoch and the same backward-to-forward ratio, pretraining the guide for half the standard main-model duration costs about 10.4 baseline-equivalent epochs. Charged to a single 80-epoch Swift run, the guide and main training together cost about 98 baseline-equivalent epochs, or 1.22 times an 80-epoch baseline. Once the guide is available, each additional main run incurs only the per-update increase of about 9 % 9\% . These model-only counts exclude the frozen representation encoder, which is shared by both methods.

sections.heading: RAEv2 guide cost.
sections.text: The RAEv2 guide costs about 37 % 37\% of a main-model forward pass, giving about 12 % 12\% extra FLOPs per main-training update. Its pretraining costs about 15 baseline-equivalent epochs. Charging that once to a 50-epoch Swift model gives a total of about 71 baseline-equivalent epochs, or 0.44 times the cost of a 160-epoch baseline under the same assumptions.

sections.heading: 11 ImageNet-256: complete results
sections.text: This appendix provides the complete ImageNet-256 results. We first report the full 19-configuration comparison with and without inference-time guidance ( Section 11.1 ), followed by the published results used in Figure 1 ( Section 11.2 ), a detailed analysis of the 875M-parameter RAEv2 model ( Section 11.3 ), training trajectories ( Section 11.4 ). Training configurations, evaluation settings, and compute accounting are given in Sections 10.1 , 10.2 and 10.3 .

sections.heading: 11.1 All configurations
sections.text: The 19 configurations consist of 18 DiffusionBench configurations (615M parameters, 80 epochs; six representation autoencoders, five VAEs, four end-to-end-tuned autoencoders, and three pixel-space models) together with the larger RAEv2 model. Across all configurations, Swift uses the same default coefficient, α = 0.4 \alpha{=}0.4 , with a smaller pretrained guide frozen before main-model training; no coefficient is tuned per configuration. Each baseline is either a reference run trained with the same schedule or a released checkpoint. In this work, we introduce Swift , a simple yet effective self-guided training method that uses a frozen weak denoiser to improve a stronger model without adding inference overhead. For each noisy input, Swift extrapolates the clean regression target away from the weak denoiser’s prediction, amplifying components that remain underfit. The weak guide can be an early training checkpoint, requires no backpropagation during main-model training, and is discarded afterward. The resulting model retains the original sampler and supports both conditional and unconditional generation without label dropout or an unconditional branch. We explain this mechanism through a spectral analysis of finite-time population gradient flow in an RKHS. With an early-stopped weak guide, we prove that a nonempty range of extrapolation strengths yields strictly lower posterior-mean error than matched standard training, despite shifting the regression target away from the posterior mean. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-256 demonstrate improvements across model scales and representations. In one ImageNet-256 configuration, Swift surpasses the baseline’s best FID using roughly half the total training compute, including guide preparation and training overhead. On RAEv2, it achieves FID 1.15 1.15 without inference-time guidance and 0.99 with guidance. These results establish target extrapolation as an effective approach to weak-to-strong diffusion training with efficient single-model inference. † † footnotetext: † \dagger Project lead ♯ Work done during internship at Alibaba 1 Introduction Diffusion models have achieved strong generative performance across images, video, and audio [ 8 , 9 , 12 ] . They are typically trained with a simple denoising regression objective, yet many of the strongest generation results rely on guidance applied only at inference [ 7 , 11 ] . In particular, autoguidance [ 11 ] shows that a deliberately weaker denoiser can improve a stronger one by defining an extrapolation direction during sampling. This suggests a broader role for weak models: rather than serving as teachers to imitate, they can provide directions along which a stronger predictor should move. Autoguidance realizes this idea by extrapolating the strong model’s prediction away from that of a smaller or less-trained counterpart [ 11 ] . Related training-time approaches instead use evolving model predictions, intermediate supervision, or guidance-conditioned objectives [ 28 , 39 , 2 , 36 ] ( Section 8 ). These developments motivate a simple question: Can weak-to-strong extrapolation be moved from inference into training, so that the final denoiser itself benefits from the correction and the weak model can be discarded afterward? We introduce Swift , a self-guided training method that uses a frozen weak denoiser to construct extrapolated regression targets. For each noisy input, instead of regressing directly toward the clean sample, Swift moves the target farther in the direction from the weak prediction toward and beyond the clean sample. The weak denoiser therefore acts as a directional reference , rather than a teacher whose output should be imitated. It can be obtained from an early checkpoint of ordinary denoising training, remains fixed during the main training run, and requires no backpropagation. After training, the guide is discarded, leaving a single denoiser and the original sampling procedure. The same construction applies to both conditional and unconditional generation. Our motivation is finite-time underfitting: because a weak denoiser has learned less of the target function, extrapolating away from its prediction can amplify directions that remain underfit. We show theoretically that, for a nonempty range of positive extrapolation strengths, deliberately shifting the training target in this way can produce a predictor strictly closer to the original posterior mean than matched standard training ( Theorem 4.1 ; proof in Section 7.4 ). 1 1.5 2 3 5 10 1.0 1.2 1.5 2.0 DiT-XL/2 SiT-XL/2 MDT REPA DDT MAR-H LightningDiT REG SFD REPA-E RAE GAE RAEv2 PAE BAR-L LightningDiT+IG SWIFT (ours) diffusion autoregressive FID-50k (no guidance) FID-50k (with guidance) ImageNet-256, published results 40 80 120 160 200 240 280 320 1.4 1.6 1.8 2 2.2 SWIFT at ep. 120: 1.50 training epoch FID-50k (no guidance) ImageNet-256, DINOv2-B (615M), w/o guidance Baseline, to ep. 320 SWIFT, α = 0.4 \alpha{=}0.4 , to ep. 240 Figure 1 : Swift reaches sub- 1.0 1.0 gFID on ImageNet-256. Dots denote raw evaluations and lines show five-point moving averages. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-256 show that the effect is not tied to a particular representation or model family. On ImageNet-256, Swift improves diffusion models built on conventional VAE latents, representation-autoencoder latents [ 38 , 26 ] , end-to-end learned latent representations, and direct pixel-space generation. Across the evaluated DiffusionBench configurations [ 16 ] , the same fixed Swift recipe lowers unguided FID in every configuration, and the improvement persists under longer training. The complete ImageNet comparisons and training trajectories are in Sections 11.1 and 11.4 , and the additional CIFAR-10 experiments are in Section 12 . When guidance is independently retuned for the baseline and Swift , the Swift model achieves lower FID in every tested configuration ( Tables 7 and 10.2 ). Our contributions are: • Weak-to-strong learning through target extrapolation. We introduce Swift , which uses a frozen weak denoiser as a directional reference to extrapolate clean-sample regression targets. The guide is fixed during main-model training and discarded at inference ( Section 2.2 ). • Broad improvements across diffusion representations. We demonstrate consistent gains across CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-256, spanning VAE, RAE, end-to-end latent, and pixel-space diffusion models. The gains persist under longer training and remain after inference-time guidance is independently retuned ( Sections 5.1 and 5.2 ). • A finite-training explanation. We therefore retain a frozen half-width guide and a fixed, moderate positive α \alpha as the simple default for the broader experiments. 6 Conclusion The regression target has received comparatively little attention as a design choice in diffusion training, yet it turns out to be a simple and effective place to intervene. By carrying the clean target past itself and away from a frozen weak model, Swift moves a weak-to-strong correction from inference into training, leaving a single denoiser and the original sampler at deployment with only about 9 % 9\% additional main-training FLOPs. Crucially, the modified target is not itself a better estimator of the posterior mean: it is deliberately biased, yet finite training on it can produce a better final predictor and better samples. This suggests a broader view of the regression target as a design interface rather than a fixed quantity—and raises the question of what other useful corrections can be written into it.
